meru-nps-circuit-breaker-buying-power:
When Korean stocks fell hard enough to halt trading, the National Pension Service used to be the buyer.
Six circuit breakers were triggered between the system's launch in December 1998 and the end of 2025, and the fund put money to work in all six.

2026 broke the pattern.
Of this year's halts, the fund chose to sell rather than buy on five of them.

@@REF@@Bourse operator issues circuit breaker for KOSPI on sharp fall (The Korea Times, 2026-07-29)|https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/economy/20260729/bourse-operator-issues-circuit-breaker-for-kospi-on-sharp-fall|https://newsimg.koreatimes.co.kr/2026/07/29/c27d7062-d511-4fc7-b806-73a17101a26e.jpg

The exchange halted trading for 20 minutes at 12:31 p.m. on July 29 after the KOSPI fell more than 8% from the previous close.
The exchange counted that halt as the eighth of the year.
The original post counts nine, and the gap appears to come from whether KOSDAQ halts are counted alongside.

## Why the fund could not buy

The National Pension Service fixes in advance how much of the total fund domestic equities may occupy, and when a rally pushes the holding above that share, it sells to bring the weight back down.
That is rebalancing.

The part that matters is not the selling but what the selling produces.
Cash trimmed during a rally is the cash available to buy during a crash.
Think of a shopping basket with a set ratio per compartment: whatever you take out of an overflowing compartment is what you spend next time.

## The rule changed in May

On May 28 the fund's management committee raised the domestic equity target from 14.9% to 20.8%.
The change answered a complaint that mechanical selling into every rally was pressing down on the market.

@@REF@@NPS raises domestic stock target to 20.8% amid market pressure (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-05-28)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/05/28/nps-raises-domestic-stock-target-to-208-percent-amid-market|https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/05/28/news-p.v1.20260528.289cd65f69e24b9fbebdbb815c4b4b16_P1.jpg

Seoul Economic Daily reported that the actual domestic equity weight sat near 30% when the decision was made.
Lifting the target by 5.9 percentage points still left the real holding more than 9 points above it.
Even with a wider allowance, the fund stayed on the selling side.

@@CHK@@Domestic equity target (through 2025)|14.9%|Domestic equity target (2026-2027)|20.8%|Increase|+5.9pp@@Widening the band by 5.9 points was meant to curb forced selling into rallies. Selling less during a rally also means banking less cash for a crash. The lack of buying power the original post points to shares a root with this rule change, separate from any judgment about fund management.@@Retrieved 2026-07-30 · NPS Fund Management Committee decision of 2026-05-28, as reported by Seoul Economic Daily and KED Global

@@CMP@@Meru's read|The fund failed to rebalance in time and missed its moment. It erased its own firepower through poor management.|KED Global's read|The wider band adopted in May to reduce forced selling into rallies also reduced the cash available to buy into a collapse.
The same fact splits on whether you read it as a management miss or as the back side of a rule changed to help the market.

@@REF@@NPS sits out Korea rout as wider equity bands blunt rebalancing (KED Global, 2026-07-29)|https://www.kedglobal.com/nps-watch/newsView/ked202607290010|https://www.kedglobal.com/data/ked/image/2026/07/29/ked202607290046.jpg

KED Global argues that the wider allocation band, introduced to curb forced selling into rallies, also dulled the fund's ability to buy aggressively into a collapse.
The same article notes that the fund made only modest purchases even on July 28, when the KOSPI closed 10.84% lower at 6,023.66.

## What the missing 219 trillion won was

At a KOSPI of 9,100 on June 19, the fund's year-to-date paper gain stood at 314 trillion won.
With the index closing at 5,663 on July 29, the same calculation gives 95 trillion won.

A paper gain is the amount written into the books for an asset that has risen in price but has not been sold.
It is not money in hand. It is an estimate of what the money would be if sold.
So when the price retreats, the entry is erased with it.

By the original post's arithmetic, delaying the fund's depletion date by one year costs 49 trillion won.
That makes 314 trillion won worth 6.4 years and 95 trillion won worth 1.9 years.

## How we will know

In the end there is one question.
Is the buying that resumed in late July the safety net returning, or simply what falls out once the weight has drifted back under the cap.

The 116 billion won bought on July 28 and 338 billion won on July 29 are far larger than the 48 billion won of June 8 or the 29 billion won of July 7.
Set against the 573 billion won of March 13, 2020, they are still small.

If the next halt brings buying in the trillions of won, the constraint has genuinely loosened. If the figure falls back to the low hundreds of billions, this week's purchases were the mechanical result of a weight that had already come down.

Acting as the market's safety net was never the fund's objective.
The objective is return, and the safety net was a by-product of chasing it.
What remains is that this year the by-product went missing.
meru-china-trs-ban-korea-chip-outflow:
Some of the foreign selling in Korean chip stocks may be Chinese money being liquidated under compulsion.
On the evening of Tuesday, June 23, China's securities regulator gave brokerages verbal guidance that blocked both new total return swap contracts on offshore stocks and the renewal of contracts coming due.

@@REF@@China securities regulator ordered cross-border swap curbs (Reuters, 2026-06-26)|https://theedgemalaysia.com/node/808450|https://assets.theedgemarkets.com/China Securities Regulatory Commission csrc 20240223_20240223184155_reuters_2.jpg

That report puts the affected book at 500 billion yuan, or 73.5 billion dollars, and says most of it sits in overseas equities.
It also confirms that contracts reaching maturity cannot be rolled over.

## What a total return swap is

A total return swap is a contract where someone else buys the stock in their own name and you collect only the gain or loss.
Put simply, the name stays with the lender and only the outcome comes back to you.

Say a Chinese private fund wants to own SK Hynix but capital controls keep it from sending dollars abroad.
It signs this contract with a foreign broker such as Goldman Sachs or Morgan Stanley, the broker buys and holds the shares under its own name, and only the price difference is settled inside China.

The money never crosses the border while the offshore gain or loss lands anyway.
With Chinese equities and property both weak, demand reportedly poured through this channel into US, Japanese and Korean technology stocks.

## Why something blocked in June is landing now

These contracts are short.
They come in one, three and six month terms, mostly three, and the way they lasted longer was by being rewritten each time they matured.

Block the renewal and the position has to be sold the moment it comes due.
Because the contracts were struck on different days, the maturities are scattered across June 23 to September 22.

Then July brought a sharp drop in AI and memory names, and with it demands for more collateral.
Anyone who could not wire dollars in time, because of the same capital controls, reportedly had no option but to sell what they held.

@@CHK@@Affected book|500bn yuan|In dollars|$73.5bn|Rollover at maturity|Blocked@@The 73.5 billion dollars in the original post is the same figure Reuters reports as 500 billion yuan, and the rollover block is confirmed separately. The premise holds up against the reporting. What no report gives is how much of that book sits in Korean names.@@Reuters 2026-06-26 and South China Morning Post 2026-06-24, press reports

## How much of it is Korean

This is the spot where the original post says it does not know.
The split of that 73.5 billion dollars by country is not disclosed.

That the money reached Korea at all, though, can be confirmed elsewhere.

@@REF@@China closes another offshore investing loophole as TRS faces restrictions (South China Morning Post, 2026-06-24)|https://www.scmp.com/business/banking-finance/article/3358240/china-closes-another-offshore-investing-loophole-trs-faces-restrictions|https://cdn.i-scmp.com/sites/default/files/styles/og_image_scmp_generic/public/d8/images/canvas/2026/06/24/9c6a0869-e0b9-4b27-a97b-6eee84c15240_2bb9333d.jpg?itok=UpOUiGkn&v=1782304513

That article names the targets of the guidance as surging US, Japanese and South Korean technology stocks, and says the funds hit hardest are private funds holding more than 30 percent of their assets in Hong Kong and US shares.
The original post could only say the Korean share was unknown. The report names Korea as one of the destinations.

One more thing splits here.
When the broker holding the position sells the shares, the Korean tape records it as foreign selling.
The money is Chinese by nationality, and the screen shows one line that says foreign.

## Where the money went instead

The cash that could not leave had somewhere to go.
CXMT, the Chinese memory maker that listed on July 27.

China needs to defend the yuan, build up artificial intelligence, make its chip supply self-sufficient and hold up its own stock market, all at once.
Read that way, this rule may be less a patch on a leak than one piece of a policy that removes the exits and pushes the money toward domestic advanced industry.

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Is the foreign selling arriving now a verdict on Korean chip earnings, or the calendar of maturities.

If the selling holds at the same intensity past September 22, the maturity explanation runs out there.
If it fades before then, much of it was the renewal ban.

Flows through these contracts are not published by country, so there is no way to carve out this channel's share of the Korean decline as a number.
Safer, then, to read it not as the cause of this selloff but as one more line on the list of causes.
jukan-microsoft-capex-175b-lease-reclass:
Microsoft now expects to spend about $175 billion on capital projects in calendar 2026.
That is below the figure the company had been carrying, and it did not get there by planning to spend less.
The spending plan stayed where it was. What changed is which accounting bucket the money lands in.

@@REF@@Microsoft extends data center lifespans to soften AI buildout costs (PYMNTS, 2026-07-29)|https://www.pymnts.com/earnings/2026/microsoft-extends-data-center-lifespans-to-soften-ai-buildout-costs/|https://www.pymnts.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/microsoft-agent-365-agentic-ai-artificial-intelligence.jpeg?w=457

## Why one quarter has two numbers
On the earnings call the company put capital expenditures for the April to June quarter at $41 billion.
The cash flow statement for the same quarter shows $35.8 billion of additions to property and equipment.
The two numbers part company over how leased facilities get counted.

@@CHK@@Capex on the call|$41.0B|Property and equipment in cash flow|$35.8B|Gap|$5.2B@@In a single quarter, $5.2 billion turns on which column it sits in. The gap appears to be the finance lease portion, and the company itself said finance leases are included in capital expenditures while operating leases are not. The premise behind the question checks out.@@2026-07-29 · Microsoft FY26 Q4 earnings release and cash flow statement

Roughly two-thirds of the quarter's spending went to short lived assets, mainly server CPUs and GPUs.
More money goes into the chips than into the shell that holds them.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/NVIDIA_GPU.jpg/960px-NVIDIA_GPU.jpg|The two-thirds. The building is now assumed to last 25 years, these boards get swapped out every few.|Mickael Courtiade · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NVIDIA_GPU.jpg

## Finance lease, operating lease
When a data center is rented rather than owned, the contract falls into one of two boxes.
A contract that works like buying on installments is a finance lease. One that works like paying rent is an operating lease.
Finance leases count as capital expenditure. Operating leases do not.

Microsoft has extended the estimated useful life of its data centers and office buildings from 15 years to 25 years, effective with fiscal 2027.
Once the asset is assumed to last 25 years, the same lease covers a smaller slice of that life, which pushes it toward the rent side.

So future data center leases move into the operating lease box, and the reported capex number gets smaller.
The chief financial officer said the greater impact is on capital expenditures.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/BalticServers_data_center.jpg/960px-BalticServers_data_center.jpg|Where the $175 billion goes. Whether the building is bought or rented decides whether the same outlay shows up as capex at all.|BalticServers.com · CC BY-SA 3.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BalticServers_data_center.jpg

## Is profit being flattered
A longer life also means a smaller depreciation charge each year, which makes profit look bigger.
The company said the change affects only the timing of future depreciation and should be a minimal benefit to fiscal 2027 operating income.
The capex line moves more than the profit line does.

The quarter itself was strong. Revenue was $90.0 billion, up 18%, and Azure passed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time.
The stock rose more than 8% after hours.

## Meta went the other way that day
Meta lifted the floor of its 2026 capital spending range from $125 billion to $130 billion and left the ceiling at $145 billion.
Second quarter revenue grew 28% to $60.8 billion, but operating margin fell from 43% to 31% and free cash flow came down to $784 million.
Microsoft's free cash flow in the same quarter was $19.6 billion.

@@REF@@Meta reports mixed Q2 results, raises low end of capex guidance range, shares move lower (Benzinga, 2026-07-29)|https://www.benzinga.com/markets/earnings/26/07/60781217/meta-reports-mixed-q2-results-raises-low-end-of-capex-guidance-range-shares-move-lower|https://cdn.benzinga.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,height=800,fit=crop/files/images/story/2026/07/29/Low-Angle-Image-Of-Meta-Logo-On-Glass-Of.jpg

Benzinga put Meta's adjusted earnings at $6.18 a share against a $7.13 estimate.
Line the two companies up and the word capex turns out to count different things at each of them.
Meta folds principal payments on finance leases into its capex figure. Microsoft's cash flow line leaves them out.

@@CMP@@Reading the lower number|$175 billion is under the old figure, so the hyperscalers are finally starting to trim AI spending.|The company's account|The spending plan is unchanged. Only the share of it counted as capex falls, because leases are being reclassified.
The stock rose 8%, so the market took the second reading. Either way, reported capex will now understate what is actually being spent.

## What settles it
The question comes down to one thing. Can the reported capex line still stand in for how much is being spent on AI.

If operating lease payments swell inside operating costs while capex stays flat, that line has stopped measuring the size of the spend.
If both rise together, the reclassification did not matter much.

For anyone selling memory or equipment, the hyperscaler capex line is the first place they look for demand.
The rule that produces that number changed quietly this week, and that will outlast the earnings beat.

Kevin Warsh, the new Fed chair, has taken the language that signals the next move on rates out of the FOMC statement altogether.

O'Halloran · Public domain|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NY_stock_exchange_traders_floor_LC-U9-10548-6.jpg

## Why these two stories sit together
Both remove information that markets had been receiving on a schedule.
The case for removal rhymes too. Quarterly reports are said to chain companies to the next three months, and Fed guidance is said to push investors into reading the committee instead of the businesses they own.
The case against rhymes as well. Take away the material prices are set on and those prices swing more and carry less information.

## Where Damodaran splits the two
He does not give the same answer twice. He would keep the quarterly report and cut the Fed's guidance.

What he would strip out of the quarterly filing is not the financial statements but the risk disclosure section and the earnings guidance companies volunteer.
The share of US listed companies issuing guidance topped half in 2003 and is now around 20%.
Reports ran 2,000 to 5,000 words in 1980 and tripled or quadrupled in size by the early 2000s.

The statements stayed the same size. The words piled up around them.

He also declines the short-termism argument. Traders with short horizons are the people standing on the other side of your order, and the mass of those trades still produces a price that holds up over a long horizon.

## Countries that dropped quarterly reports
The European Union made quarterly reporting mandatory in 2007 and withdrew it in 2013.
Britain and Singapore added it and then backed away, and Japan ended its quarterly filing requirement in 2024.
The same experiment has run in several places and has mostly been reversed.

## Why he lands the other way on the Fed
His reason for backing less Fed guidance is his own reading that the Fed is not what sets the direction of rates.
Measured from January 1962 through June of this year, the Fed funds rate goes up or down after short term Treasury rates have already moved.
Most of the variation in long rates, he adds, is explained by inflation and real growth.

If that holds, cutting back on advance signals removes less information than it appears to.

@@REF@@Fed policymakers leave rates unchanged, three officials dissent in favour of a hike (Fox Business, 2026-07-29)|https://www.foxbusiness.com/economy/federal-reserve-interest-rate-decision-july-29-2026|https://a57.foxnews.com/static.foxbusiness.com/foxbusiness.com/content/uploads/2026/06/0/0/fed-chair-kevin-warsh-first-press-conference.jpg?ve=1&tl=1

The day the post went up, 29 July, happened to be the first test of that experiment.
The Fed held its policy rate at 3.50% to 3.75% on a 9 to 3 vote, and all three dissents were for a quarter point increase.

The statement carried no line about where rates go next.
With the signal gone, what showed through was the spread of views inside the committee.

## What we will be watching
The question comes down to one thing. What fills the space that disclosure and guidance leave behind.

If financial statements and inflation and growth data fill it, Damodaran's reading was right.
If investors who cannot wait six months fill it with private data sets and readings of central bank remarks, the information did not shrink. It moved somewhere more expensive.

For an individual investor that difference matters.
A public filing reaches everyone on the same day at the same price. What replaces it reaches whoever paid for it first.
semianalysis-modular-datacenter-labor-bo:
The largest datacenters in the world are now going up as factory-built blocks that crews bolt together on site.
Concrete walls arrive as finished panels. Electrical and mechanical rooms arrive already wired.
Sometimes an entire data hall arrives on the back of a truck.

This is not a choice about saving money.
There is nobody left on site to build the old way.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/BalticServers_data_center.jpg/960px-BalticServers_data_center.jpg|The electrical rooms and piping that go inside a hall like this are increasingly assembled in a factory and trucked in.|BalticServers.com · CC BY-SA 3.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BalticServers_data_center.jpg

## Why electricians are the bottleneck

Electrical work carries a large share of a datacenter build.
The original piece estimates that electricians account for 30-40% of total construction man hours on a project.

And the supply of electricians does not jump because someone offers more money.
Licensing takes years, and people keep leaving the trade in the meantime.

@@REF@@Data center boom strains Texas homebuilders' need for electricians (The Texas Tribune, 2026-04-28)|https://www.texastribune.org/2026/04/28/data-centers-texas-electricians-builders/|https://i0.wp.com/www.texastribune.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/20260422-Texas-Electricians-RE-01.jpg?fit=2560%2C1707&quality=100&ssl=1&w=1200&h=630

The Texas Tribune reports roughly 71,000 electricians working in Texas, with about 20,000 leaving the workforce nationally each year.
One in three is already between 50 and 70 years old.

Datacenters pay $35 an hour plus overtime and per diem, while a small homebuilder can offer $20.
An Abilene homebuilder said his projects slipped by two months as a result.

@@CHK@@US electrician employment (2024)|818,700|Projected 10-year growth (2024-2034)|9%|Projected annual openings|about 81,000@@Nine percent over a decade is roughly one percent a year. Most of those 81,000 annual openings exist to backfill retirements and departures rather than to add headcount. Doubling the wage does not move the number of licensed bodies past that pace. The premise that this is a bottleneck money cannot clear holds up in the statistics.@@Retrieved 2026-07-30 · US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook (electricians)

## What actually moves into the factory

Anything built off site and delivered ready to install is prefabrication.
Only the self-contained pieces, rooms and boxes that ship complete and get bolted to each other, count as modular.
Every modular unit is prefabricated, but not everything prefabricated is modular.

Why is that distinction a money question.
Because the share of work moved into a factory is the share of people you can pull off the site.

Pouring concrete in place means each layer has to reach roughly 75% of its design strength before the next one goes on top.
Panels cured in a factory skip that wait entirely.

## So how much faster

The original piece rebuilds vendor claims from the bottom up and estimates that modular construction compresses the build window by about 36%, or 7-9 months, and lands about 8% cheaper on capex per megawatt.
It also estimates that equipment vendors grow their take per project from roughly $3.5 million per megawatt to roughly $7 million.

@@REF@@AI data center boom strains global construction capacity (Data Center Knowledge, 2026-07-22)|https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-construction/ai-data-center-boom-strains-global-construction-capacity|https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt8eb3cdfc1fce5194/blt15bd6c442075c404/6a5fee64b534f51ac8ba9251/Data-Center-Construction-Getty.jpg?disable=upscale&width=1200&height=630&fit=crop

Data Center Knowledge reports that more than 70% of markets globally describe datacenter contractor capacity as tightening or overstretched, and that nearly 90% of respondents named shortages in mechanical, electrical and plumbing trades.
The same survey puts the onsite labor saving from prefabricated electrical skids and power rooms at 20-40%.
That says the bottleneck in the original piece belongs to the whole industry, not to one company's schedule.

@@CMP@@The common read|What stops a datacenter is power and transformers. Get the electricity to the site and money solves the rest.|SemiAnalysis's read|Power eventually gets solved. What money cannot solve is the number of licensed electricians and pipefitters.
The same word, bottleneck, splits on which constraint money can actually clear.

## How we will know

In the end there is one question.
Does modular genuinely route around the labor shortage, or does it move the bottleneck into the factory.

Factory assembly is done by people too.
Factory work is easier to staff than licensed electrical work on a live site, though, and repetition builds skill faster.

The original piece expects modular to pass 30% of total live capacity by the end of 2028.
If completion dates hold through 2027 even where electricians are short, modular really did route around the constraint. If modular share climbs while schedules slip anyway, the bottleneck simply moved indoors.

In the datacenter story, the things that get priced are usually chips and power.
From this year, the number of people available to put up the building sits in the same place.
kobeissi-fed-hold-three-hike-dissents:
The Fed left its benchmark rate at 3.50% to 3.75%.
It is the fifth straight hold since December, and the longest pause since the 2008 cycle.

The vote was 9-3.
All three who voted against wanted the rate raised by a quarter point.

@@REF@@Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady, but 3 officials vote for hike (CBS News, 2026-07-29)|https://www.cbsnews.com/news/federal-reserve-interest-rates-kevin-warsh-july-206/|https://assets1.cbsnewsstatic.com/hub/i/r/2026/07/28/48af98d6-8181-4f05-9ab9-09083d5d2750/thumbnail/1200x630/1f10b38e2fee2c59d9e0e5f67bfe448f/gettyimages-2285454193.jpg

## Why hawkish dissents are the unusual kind
Dissents at the Fed usually come from the easing side.
Someone worries about growth and argues for a cut.

This time all three went the other way.
Beth Hammack (Cleveland), Neel Kashkari (Minneapolis) and Lorie Logan (Dallas) run regional Fed banks, and each wanted a hike.

No one on the Washington board voted against.
The pressure to tighten came from the districts, not from the center.

## What the split is actually about
The statement itself says it.
Inflation stays above the 2% goal in part because of supply shocks in certain sectors, energy among them, in the Fed's own words.

A supply shock is a price rise caused by there being less of something, not by more buyers.
Raising rates makes borrowing dearer and cools demand, but it does not put back the barrels the Middle East conflict took out.
Read the same inflation number as a supply story and waiting is right; read it as expectations hardening and hiking is right.

@@CMP@@The three who wanted a hike|Inflation has sat above the target for a long time already. Move before expectations harden.|The nine who held|This round of inflation was pushed up by an energy supply shock. A higher policy rate does not produce more crude.
Both sides point at the same sentence, and split on where the inflation comes from.

## What markets disliked was not the decision
Chair Kevin Warsh declined to say what comes next.

Did the Fed take an explicit change in its policy rate today, he asked, and answered: no, but he thinks that is the beginning of the story, not the end of the story.
Five-plus years of inflation above target, he added, cannot be cured in nine weeks or by one month of softening inflation.

@@REF@@'The Fed's on the case,' Chair Warsh says as rate pause holds (Real Estate News, 2026-07-29)|https://www.realestatenews.com/2026/07/29/the-feds-on-the-case-chair-warsh-says-as-rate-pause-holds|https://images.ctfassets.net/hzfwsdcegxo2/49df8WKo2acn2bPh8Bp2S4/16e485e74c0419fc0f76439d99ee5f66/012826_-_REN_-_Fed_January_meeting.png?w=1200&h=630&fit=fill

This is what it means to drop forward guidance.
Forward guidance was the habit of telling markets in advance which way the policy rate would lean.
Without it, traders have to price each meeting themselves right up to the announcement, and the money doing that piles onto one side and unwinds again.

On decision day the S&P 500 changed direction three times, with roughly $2.9 trillion of market value moving across those swings.
The policy rate did not move, yet the 30-year Treasury yield pushed above 5.2%, its highest since 2007.

@@REF@@30-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2007 after Fed keeps rates unchanged (CNBC, 2026-07-29)|https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/29/treasury-yields-fed-interest-rates.html|https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108295278-1776860361515-gettyimages-2271888399-warsh_senate_517_042126.jpeg?v=1778700082&w=1920&h=1080

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/NYSE127.jpg/500px-NYSE127.jpg|Three reversals in one session. When the Fed stops saying what comes next, the pricing work moves onto the floor.|Ryan Lawler · Public domain|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NYSE127.jpg

## So what settles it
The question comes down to one thing.
Is this inflation made by supply, or by expectations that have hardened.

If the energy shock fades and prices stay high, the three who wanted a hike were right; if crude calms and inflation comes down with it, the nine who waited were right.
Before that, the first signal is whether the hawkish dissents grow to four or more in September.

The policy rate stood still and thirty-year money still got its dearest since 2007. That says the handle the Fed is holding is shorter than it looks.

## How a price target is built
A price target is where an analyst expects the stock to trade, usually within a year.
The arithmetic is plain: take the earnings per share the company is expected to make, and multiply by the multiple such a company is judged to deserve.

Change either of those two numbers and the answer moves a long way.
So cutting an earnings estimate while raising a target is not, arithmetically, a contradiction.

## How you cut this year and lift the target anyway
You move the base year forward by one.

As of early July, the estimates on the table put SK hynix's 2026 operating profit at 289.4 trillion won and 2027 at 470 trillion, making next year 1.6 times this one.
Shift the base of the calculation from 2026 to 2027 and the target rises even as this year's figure comes down.

## Why 6 times earnings does not hold the stock up
In a cyclical business like memory, the multiple looks cheapest exactly when profit is highest.
The denominator is at its peak.

Think of an air-conditioner shop. Value it on the books from a scorching August and it always looks cheap; the question is whether September brings the same profit.
What the market doubts is not the 6.0 multiple. It is the 470 trillion won of next-year profit the multiple was applied to.

## What is moving the price right now is not valuation
Second-quarter operating profit came in at 60.5 trillion won, more than six times a year earlier, and still short of the 64 trillion consensus.

The shares fell more than 13% after the results and now sit below half the intraday high of June 26.
What sets the price today is the pace of forced selling, not next year's earnings estimate.

## So what settles it
The question comes down to one thing.
Is the gap of more than three times between target and price made by the market's fear, or by the analysts' optimism?

If memory prices hold and the 2027 estimate survives, the houses raising targets were right; if that estimate starts coming down, earnings and multiple fall together and the gap closes from the target side rather than the price side.
The first signal is whether the brokers touch their 2027 numbers.

A price target is not a prophecy. It is a written-down assumption, and the useful part is not the 4.7 million won but what has to be true next year for that number to stand.

meru-ukraine-defense-chief-purge:
A country at war fired its defense minister and, six days later, replaced its top general as well.
That happened in Ukraine on July 15 and July 21.

@@REF@@Ukraine's reformist defense minister is out after six months, and earlier his audit exposed $7.2 billion in defense overspending (Euromaidan Press, 2026-07-15)|https://euromaidanpress.com/2026/07/15/ukraines-reformist-defense-minister-is-out-after-six-months-earlier-his-audit-exposed-7-2-billion-in-defense-overspending/|https://euromaidanpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/photo_2026-04-15_13-36-04.jpg

The piece lays out what Mykhailo Fedorov did in six months on the job.
An internal audit of the ministry turned up $7.2 billion of overspending, weapons procurement moved to open tenders, and ministry staff were put through polygraph tests.
Meru puts the overspending at $6.7 billion, a slightly different count of the same audit.

Most coverage framed the shake-up as a clash of doctrine, a 35-year-old minister betting on drones against a 60-year-old general raised on infantry warfare.
That is not where the break actually ran.

## Why the two became rivals rather than boss and subordinate

After losing Crimea in 2014, Ukraine adopted NATO-style civilian control, putting a civilian defense minister in charge of supervising the military.
On the org chart the minister now sat above the commander-in-chief.

The reporting line was left as it was.
Both men kept reporting directly to the president and taking their orders from him.

Move it into a company and it reads clearly.
You put the head of investments in charge of supervising the head of trading, then have the chief executive grade both of them personally.
To the head of trading, the head of investments is not a boss. He is a competitor.

## Why the arrangement held for twelve years

Where the boundaries of authority are vague, a person usually fills the gap.
Andriy Yermak, the president's chief of staff, was that person.
When the minister and the general collided, the president's office settled it, and when parliament balked, Yermak settled that.

In November 2025 Yermak resigned over a corruption scandal in the energy sector.
His successor could not do the same work, and the president's office lost its grip on parliament.
In a chamber where 226 votes are a majority, the bloc that reliably followed the president shrank from about 250 members to about 130.

A structure held up by a person rather than by rules shows its blueprint the moment that person leaves.

## Why 16% is the number that matters

What Fedorov touched was procurement.
He moved 155mm artillery shells to competitive tender, and the price came down 16%.

@@REF@@Procurement of 155-mm ammunition for the armed forces via tender saved 16% of allocated funds (Militarnyi, 2026-05-21)|https://militarnyi.com/en/news/procurement-of-155-mm-ammunition-ukraine/|https://militarnyi.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/155-mm-snaryad-1-1024x576.jpg

That report carries the figure Fedorov gave journalists himself in May.
Buying the same shells in the same quantity for 16% less does not mean the shells got cheaper.
It means someone had been taking that 16% off the top.

So the reform saved budget and cut off an income stream in the same motion.

## Why a capable minister becomes dangerous

@@CMP@@The common reading|A young drone-first minister collided with an old infantry general, and the president sided with the army|Meru's reading|In a system with no clear boundary of authority, a minister pushing reform cannot be checked by legal means, so he is removed instead

Same dismissal. One side sees a fight over doctrine, the other sees an empty box in the institutional design.

Protests began on July 16, the day after the dismissal.
Veterans and serving soldiers led them, and they spread to more than sixteen cities.
On July 21 President Zelenskyy met the demand, dismissed Syrskyi and appointed 43-year-old Mykhailo Drapatyi in his place.

@@REF@@Ukraine overhauls its military top brass for the fight against Russia (NPR, 2026-07-21)|https://www.npr.org/2026/07/21/g-s1-134849/ukraine-military-chief-fired-protests|https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims3/default/strip/false/crop/5747x3233+0+300/resize/1400/quality/85/format/jpeg/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2F7a%2F6c%2F406b76d44540921843b4d9c347bc%2Fap26202419840471.jpg

In that report Syrskyi points to 743 square kilometers retaken this year as his record, and Fedorov calls Drapatyi a voice for change.
The minister's chair is still empty, the confirmation vote delayed by the protests.

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Was this a chain of command being tidied up, or a reform being rolled back.

If open tenders widen to drone procurement under Drapatyi and a new minister is confirmed, the first reading holds.
If procurement slides back behind closed doors and the ministry stays without a minister, this was the point where the reform stopped.

Where institutions work, a capable minister is an asset to the state.
Where they do not, there is no legal way to check him, and a capable minister turns into a threat.

Unwinding a position bought with borrowed money is called deleveraging.
When prices fall, the borrower runs short of collateral and has to sell, and that selling pushes prices lower, which forces the next sale.

This kind of selling does not look at whether a company is good or bad.
The size of the position decides what gets sold, so strong results get dumped alongside weak ones.

From July 31, buying a single-stock leveraged ETF in Korea requires 30 million won of cash sitting in the account.

Professional investor is a status the Capital Markets Act grants on the basis of holdings and income.
The name sounds like it asks about your job.
What it actually looks at is money.

The base requirement is a month-end average balance above 50 million won, held for at least one year out of the past five.

The product existed in Hong Kong first.

Is taking retail out of this product protection, or is it a push toward the place supervision cannot follow.

If only the domestic side shrinks while Hong Kong grows, the risk was not removed.

Which of the two arrives first is what decides what this rule actually is.

jukan-skhynix-hbm-2027-lta-price-cap:
SK hynix is negotiating the volumes and prices of the HBM it will sell in 2027 with its major customers right now.
The answer came in the Q&A that followed its second-quarter results on the 28th.

The answer itself was short, that talks are going smoothly. The more useful part came next.
The long-term supply agreements already signed are not contracts that nail a price down to one number.

## Does HBM follow DRAM prices?

The company said conventional DRAM average selling prices rose about 30% from the previous quarter, and NAND rose by the mid-50s in percentage terms.
So the question was whether HBM prices simply ride along.

The answer was that it does not work that way.
Building one HBM stack eats more wafers than plain DRAM of the same capacity, and adds the TSV step that drills through stacked dies to connect them, plus extra packaging.
So prices are set customer by customer, weighing not only conventional DRAM pricing and supply and demand but the resources and the opportunity cost that go into HBM.

Opportunity cost here means the money the same production line would have earned making something else.
When DRAM prices jump, what the company gives up to make HBM instead grows too, and so does its ground for charging more.

while the detailed equipment inspection and damage assessment are still under way.

@@REF@@TSMC's Kumamoto fab moving back to normal operation in stages (ITmedia NEWS, 2026-07-29)|https://www.itmedia.co.jp/news/article/2607/29/2000000266/|https://www.itmedia.co.jp/news/article/ogp/2607/29/2000000266/10001260/2048

@@REF@@Kumamoto hit by intensity 7, activity still elevated, one week of caution urged (NHK, 2026-07-29)|https://news.web.nhk/newsweb/na/na-k10015189251000|https://imgu.web.nhk/news/u/news/html/20260729/K10015189251_2607290408_0729040929_01_02.jpg

## Why one week specifically

Ten years ago in this same Kumamoto, a strong quake at intensity 7 came first.
People took it for the mainshock.
Two days later a larger one, the real mainshock, hit.

The first tremor had not been the main event but the leading edge of a bigger one, what seismologists call a foreshock.
That is why the agency says this quake looks like the 2016 sequence.

## Where this quake came from

Most earthquakes happen where one slab of the earth's crust grinds under another.
That boundary is called a subduction zone, and the very large quakes tend to originate there.

This one did not. It came from a crack inside Kyushu itself.
A crack that can move again is called an active fault, and the one that moved here appears to be the Hinagu fault zone.

@@REF@@The Kumamoto earthquake (M7.1) of July 28, 2026 (Japan Society for Active Fault Studies, 2026-07-28)|https://jsaf.info/jishin/2026/07/20260728202045.html

The Philippine Sea plate slides under the Eurasian plate here at four to six centimeters a year, loading that fault for centuries.
Like a balloon that keeps taking air until it bursts, a fault that has been holding finally slips all at once, and that slip is the earthquake.

This epicenter sits about 20 kilometers south of the 2016 epicenter.
If the 2016 quake released the stress stored in the northern stretch of the fault, this one appears to have released the southern stretch.

## What happened outside the fab

Twenty-eight sections of stone wall collapsed at Kumamoto Castle.
Ten people are unaccounted for after a gas leak at an Aeon mall.
At a paper plant in Yatsushiro, two people were found in cardiac arrest and nine are missing.

Kikuyo Town holds JASM's two fabs along with Sony and Fujifilm facilities inside the same 20-kilometer radius.
One plant holding up is not the same as the region holding up.

## So what actually settles this

It comes down to one question.
Was this the end of it, or the leading edge of something larger the way 2016 was.

If no bigger quake arrives within the week and the aftershocks fade, JASM's staged restart holds.
If another quake of this size or larger hits, everything resets: the building checks that looked finished, the detailed equipment inspection, the restart schedule.

When a fab stops and starts repeatedly, the loss does not scale with downtime alone.
Each restart drags the inspection and requalification steps along with it again.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is raising prices on certain MLCC products by 30% for shipments made on or after August 1, 2026.
The move came in a notice sent to customers,
and it applies to every MLCC product under the pricing code the company manages as one group.

## What an MLCC is, and why 30% matters

Open up a phone and you find hundreds of parts smaller than a grain of rice sitting on the board.
Most of them are MLCCs.

The part holds a small charge and releases it on demand, smoothing out the voltage,
so that when a chip suddenly draws a burst of current the supply does not sag or spike.

Equipment that draws more power needs more of them.
A high-end AI server carries more than ten times the MLCC count of a smartphone.
Each one is cheap, but the sheer number means a single price step lands directly in the cost of a server.

## How this differs from the last increase

MLCC prices already moved once this spring.
Taiyo Yuden raised prices on some products from May 1, and the reason it gave then was the rising cost of gold and silver.
Samsung Electro-Mechanics, which holds roughly 23% of the global market, stayed put.

@@REF@@Exclusive: Japan's Taiyo Yuden raises MLCC prices, will Murata and Samsung Electro-Mechanics follow? (Dailian, 2026-04-15)|https://www.dailian.co.kr/news/view/1633952|https://cdnimage.dailian.co.kr/news/202604/news_1776236124_1633952_m_1.jpeg

That report described an industry waiting on Murata, the market leader, to speak at its earnings call.
Whatever the top maker said about pricing would set the direction for everyone else.
Three months later the one that moved first was the number two, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and the step was 30%.

The reason it gave is also different from the spring.
Instead of input costs, the company pointed to structural growth in electronics demand putting pressure on the supply chain beyond what it can absorb internally.

If raw materials are the reason, falling input costs eventually give a company grounds to walk the price back.
If demand is the reason, no such grounds exist.

## Delivery dates bind before prices do

Taiyo Yuden paired its increase with a warning that it may not be able to meet the delivery schedules customers request.
That is the company saying supply will fall short of demand even after the price goes up.

Prices can be negotiated. Delivery dates cannot.
It also means the thing keeping a server from shipping on time may not be a GPU but a component smaller than a fingernail.

## So what actually settles this

It comes down to one question.
Does the 30% harden into real contract prices, or does it stay a notice.

If August shipments bill at the new prices and Murata joins the round of increases,
pricing power has moved from the buyers of these parts to the makers of them.
If customers instead delay orders or shift volume elsewhere and the increase sticks only on part of the lineup,
the notice will have been a negotiating card.

The heavier line is not the one about raising prices. It is the one about not being able to supply enough even at the higher price.
The shortage the AI buildout created appears to have worked its way past GPUs and memory down to the cheapest layer of the bill of materials.

On July 28, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) moved to block imports of new Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots.
As Serenity's post said, Reuters had the exclusive.

But the actual measure doesn't stop at robots.
An inverter is the device that turns the direct current from solar panels or batteries into the alternating current the grid runs on.
Inverters were added to the ban too.
The companies named as targets are Unitree, a robot maker, and Sungrow and Huawei, both inverter makers.

Serenity's post framed this as a move "to protect American Humanoid/Robotics programs."
What officials actually said reads differently.

An administration official said the US needs independent and secure supply chains for critical and emerging technologies like robotic devices and power inverters.
The risk being targeted is data theft and cyberattacks, not competition.

At announcement, no specific US company was being named as a clear beneficiary.
If the exemptions end up broad, Chinese-made components can keep arriving through side doors.
If they end up narrow, domestic robot and inverter manufacturing could actually speed up.

It argues the real fault line isn't infrastructure versus applications at all, it's how replaceable the software is.

Products with low switching costs and thin proprietary data, mostly seat-priced interface tools, are easy for an AI agent to replace.
Systems embedded deep in a business, even some vertical software running banking or retail operations, are harder to dislodge no matter the category label.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing:
is this split really about what a company sells, or about how it charges for it?

If it's mostly an industry story, infrastructure and security software should keep outperforming almost regardless of pricing model.

If it's mostly a pricing-model story, some vertical software that has already moved away from flat per-seat licensing toward usage-based or outcome-based pricing should hold up better than this week's index split suggests.
Some 'infrastructure' names still selling by the seat should eventually feel the same pressure.

Next quarter's earnings season, when more companies disclose how their pricing models are shifting,
will start to answer which read is closer to right.

What that actually means is watching the pricing model, not the industry label.
Software sold under flat per-seat licensing carries the same AI-substitution risk whether it calls itself infrastructure or application software, as long as switching costs stay low.

An application-software name that has already moved to usage- or outcome-based pricing, on the other hand, may hold up better than this quarter's index drop implies.
The one thing to check next earnings season is which application-software companies disclose a shift away from per-seat pricing, since those could be undervalued relative to this index gap.

Don't read the infrastructure and security label itself as a safety signal, either.
Some names in that category are still selling by the seat, and they carry the same exposure.

## Why a capacitor is chip news
This part is smaller than a fingernail. It is called a capacitor.
It stores a small burst of electricity and releases it to keep power steady inside a circuit.

A single server board holds thousands of them,
and the ones built by stacking ceramic layers are called MLCCs.

AI servers draw far more power and tolerate far less noise than a regular PC,
so they need many more MLCCs, and better ones.

## What actually happened
TrendForce data cited by Jukan shows June shipments from Murata,
Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Taiyo Yuden hit their highest level in five years.
AI demand is what pushed their production lines there.

Prices moved with them.

and spot prices climbed as much as three times their earlier level.

## Why the shortage hit now
The cause is not demand alone. It is allocation.
Murata, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Taiyo Yuden are shifting lines
that used to make consumer-grade parts (X5R) toward the higher AI-grade spec (X6S, X7R).

A factory cannot double its output overnight,
so a line that gains capacity on one side gives it up on the other.

The parts actually running short are mid-capacity capacitors (1 to 22 microfarads)
used in ordinary appliances and cars.

## Who fills the gap the big three leave
This is the part Jukan's post does not mention.
As the big three chase AI orders,
Taiwan's Yageo and Walsin Technology are stepping into the consumer-grade orders they leave behind.

Is this a structural bottleneck that rides the AI server boom for several quarters,
or a temporary supply knot that unwinds once inventory rebuilds.

stay above 1.25 through Q3 and Q4, the structural read holds.
If the inventory that fell below 30 days returns to normal by year-end, this was a knot, not a wall.

That clustering is the result of Japan's push to rebuild its chip industry by concentrating new capacity around Kumamoto.
The 2011 Tohoku disaster taught the industry not to pack a supply chain into one region, yet the same structure repeated itself here.

Memory now makes up 26% of the total bill-of-materials cost in Nvidia's next-gen AI server rack, Vera Rubin, according to Morgan Stanley. On the prior generation, Grace Blackwell, that share was just 9%.
Chip analyst Jukan relayed the shift, citing checks from Taiwan's Fubon Securities and other research desks.

Per Fubon, Micron ($MU) channel checks suggest Nvidia's HBM4 cost will rise to $31-32 per gigabyte, from $17-18 for HBM3E in 2026.
That's also pushing estimates for a single Rubin GPU's price toward $78,000-$80,000.

## Why did memory get this expensive

Morgan Stanley pegs the bill-of-materials for one rack, 72 GPUs across 36 superchips, at about $7.8 million.
GPUs account for roughly $4 million of that (up 57% from Blackwell), and memory (HBM4 plus LPDDR5X) comes to about $2 million.
Memory cost just $373,900 on Grace Blackwell, so it's jumped more than fivefold.

Per the checks Jukan relayed, Nvidia plans to keep the rack's basic layout unchanged (72 GPUs, cable for scale-up, optical for scale-out) despite the cost jump.
The reason is token economics. Blackwell processes about 80,000 tokens per second at 150 megawatts; Rubin does roughly 800,000 tokens per second in the same power envelope, about 10 times more.
For cloud providers, that means even pricier GPUs can still pencil out if cost per token keeps falling.

## Other chipmakers hit the same wall

The checks Jukan relayed also covered Google and Intel.
Google reportedly plans to deploy 12-15 million of its own AI chips (TPUs) by 2028, when it moves to a ninth-generation TPU with four compute dies, more than doubling throughput.
Intel's advanced packaging (EMIB) capacity is expected to double, from 10,000-12,000 units by the end of this year to 24,000-25,000 by the end of next year.
The memory and packaging bottleneck isn't unique to Nvidia.

## What actually settles this
It comes down to one thing.
How much of the memory cost increase gets offset by falling cost per token.

Here's the test.
If cloud providers take delivery of Rubin on schedule, shipments in Q3 and volume ramp in Q4, the token-economics logic wins.
If deployment gets delayed or scaled back, memory costs were the real drag.
